title: Trehan to Young Indians: Get a Heart Check-Up Before 25
excerpt: On World Heart Day, leading cardiologists told PTI that heart disease is striking Indians younger — and that screening should start at 25 or 30, not in middle age.
body:
• Speaking to PTI on World Heart Day, cardiac surgeon Dr Naresh Trehan set a concrete rule: if there is a family history of heart disease and diabetes, get a check-up before age 25; even without one, get a comprehensive check-up before 30.
  • Cardiovascular disease contributes to nearly one-fourth of all deaths in India, and younger adults are increasingly hit by heart attacks and cardiac arrests — doctors say blood pressure and cholesterol screening should start in the 20s, not middle age.
  • Indians carry a higher baseline risk than Western populations: lower protective HDL cholesterol, higher rates of type 2 diabetes, more abdominal fat and a greater hypertension risk, says Dr L.K. Jha of Asian Hospital, Faridabad.
  • The experts' prescription is unglamorous but specific: physical activity, a shift away from the nutrition transition toward Western diets, tobacco control, and moving preventive cardiology from symptom-driven to risk-based care.

The New Timeline for Screening

The headline recommendation from this year's World Heart Day commentary, observed globally on September 29, is a number: 25. "If there is a family history of heart disease and diabetes, you should get a check-up before the age of 25," Trehan, chairman and managing director of Medanta, told PTI. "Even those without a family history should undergo a comprehensive health check-up before 30."

Cardiac surgeons increasingly see patients who thought heart disease was someone else's problem. "Honestly, heart disease is endemic in India and around the world," said renowned heart surgeon Dr Shriram Nene. "We need to shift the discussion from acute care to prevention, early recognition and early treatment."

Why Indians Are at Higher Risk

The biology is unflattering. "Compared to Western populations, Indians usually have lower levels of protective HDL cholesterol, higher rates of type 2 diabetes, more belly fat, and a greater risk of high blood pressure," said Dr L.K. Jha, Associate Director and Head of Unit-II Cardiology at Asian Hospital, Faridabad. That combination means a young Indian may feel completely healthy while carrying several interacting cardiovascular risk factors — which is why consultant interventional cardiologist Dr Ashish Mishra argues preventive cardiology should move "from a symptom-driven approach to a risk-based approach."

Public health researcher Prof Monika Arora of the Public Health Foundation of India traced the surge to lifestyle: "The increase in cardiovascular diseases we are seeing in India is a result of our changing lifestyles and the nutrition transition that our country has experienced, where we have moved from traditional diets to Western diets." Desk jobs, long commutes, screen time, workplace stress, tobacco including vapes, trans fats and air pollution all compound the metabolic load.

The Prescription

"On World Heart Day, we should pay attention to our own health, specifically our heart health. We know that India has a very high incidence of heart attacks, and a large number of people die from them," said Trehan. "Today, I would like to focus on metabolic health," added Dr Amit Gupta of the Global Metabolic Health Alliance — blood pressure, cholesterol, fatty liver and body weight, "which together determine our metabolic health."

Cardiologist Dr Anand Ram of Apex Group of Hospitals listed the warning signs that should never be waved away: chest discomfort, breathlessness, unusual sweating, sudden fatigue or palpitations. And prevention, he stressed, "is not a one-day effort — it is a lifelong commitment to better heart health." Advances like genome sequencing, family-history mapping and biochemical profiling can now build an individual risk picture — but only if people show up for the check-up in the first place.

Diaspora Angle

The genetic risk profile doesn't change at the airport. Diaspora families in Surrey, Edison or Sydney — eating Western diets and often skipping the screenings their grandparents never got — face the same compounded risk, making Trehan's before-25/before-30 rule as relevant abroad as in Surat.
